extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, instrument makers, astronomers, and Royal Society readers (17th-century scientific practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and procedural standards for constructing and using scientific instruments (barometer/baroscope), performing observational astronomy (eclipses, comets, occultations), casting very thin metal statues, and modelling air resistance as described in 17th-century Philosophical Transactions reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Barometer division enlargement (Hook's baroscope design)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct a baroscope composed of cylinders and tubes (A, B, BC) sized so that the upper part of cylinder B is 29 inches plus such a part of the height of tube BC as the specific gravity of the liquor in BC is to that of mercury below the line ab in cylinder A; make cylinder C as high as desired. The square of the diameter of tube BC should be to the square of the diameter of cylinder B or C as the rise of the mercury in B is to the whole length of BC so the divisions are enlarged optimally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer larger diameter for cylinder A (need not be above 1 inch long). Arrange diameters so nothing is superfluous and the enlarged divisions are maximised. The design causes liquid columns (spirit + oil) to amplify mercury motion so small atmospheric changes produce large visible displacements. Ensure the heights and cross-sectional proportions follow the described geometric relation for maximal enlargement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical filling and evacuation procedure for Hook's baroscope
rubrics_metrics.description: Fill and evacuate the assembled instrument using temporary holes: leave a small hole at the top of cylinder A and another near the top of cylinder B; pour in mercury via A until both tubes reach the hole level, then seal A and open B to draw off mercury from BC until it will run no longer, then stop B so cylinder A is evacuated of air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After evacuation, pour into BC a coloured spirit of wine (cochineal) mixed with oil of turpentine (equal parts) to the chosen enlarged-scale height (each 13 feet of oil+spirit raises mercury ~10 inches). Finally pour mercury via BC to set mercury surfaces so that at the extreme expected limits (in England ~30.6 and 28.6 inches) the mercury remains within the bodies of the cylinders and never enters the thin tubes. Seal holes hermetically (e.g., sealing-wax) when required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction for thermal expansion in baroscope readings
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for dilatation and contraction of the spirit of wine (or other liquor) by hanging a thermometer containing the same liquor whose tube is as near as possible of the same diameter as tube BC; use its descent and ascent to correct baroscope readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the thermometer's movement and add or subtract that amount from baroscope changes to achieve rigorous exactness. Also consider investigating whether mercury itself shrinks or swells with temperature and whether that would obviate the correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wheel-barometer limitations and anti-patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Wheel-barometer (earlier invention) is prone to defects: mercury adheres to glass causing jerks (rise/fall all at once), it's difficult to adjust, and is apt to be out of order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of these limitations, the wheel-barometer has been largely laid aside; prefer designs (like Hook's baroscope) that avoid adhesion-caused jerks and are easier to adjust for more exact measurements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational timing practice for eclipses and occultations
rubrics_metrics.description: Record the beginning and end times of eclipses/occultations using a pendulum clock corrected by fixed stars; note the penumbral/contact events precisely (e.g., times to the minute/second).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take times by a pendulum clock and correct clock time using observations of fixed stars to verify timing. Record the extent of eclipse (quantified, e.g., in digits) and note observational conditions. For occultations, specify moments of limb contact and immersion/emersion times with as fine temporal resolution as possible (e.g., to seconds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for positional comet observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine comet positions relative to known stars using a micrometer, record angular separations and directions, and compute celestial coordinates (longitude and latitude) from those measures and observed stellar positions/heights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe and record date/time, constellation and nearby reference stars, measure distance from named stars with the micrometer (e.g., 1° by micrometer), measure altitude of a reference star to verify times, and make repeated observations when possible. Report apparent motion (degrees per day), tail characteristics, and changes in brightness or latitude. Use multiple nights to triangulate longitude/latitude; verify timekeeping via stellar altitude observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of casting statues of extraordinary thinness
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a fired-clay core of the desired figure; create shallow holes in the core and insert small metal pieces fixed with clay to keep core and mould separated. Scrape the core to the intended thickness, coat with a metal-friendly earth, lay on a layer of yellow wax mixed with pitch/rosin to form the desired statue thickness, then add small and large wax channels so that small channels enter large channels which all meet at a pouring hole; cover with fireproof clay and burn out the wax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small metal pieces (anchors) prevent core and mould touching when the wax runs out. Arrange little channels (for distribution) to feed into great channels which converge to one pouring hole (e). Include air vents (ff) and holes at the foot (gg) to allow wax to run out during burning. Burn the mould red hot; when cool, stop foot-holes gg, bury mould in a pit and pour very well-melted metal. For very thin statues, mix copper with a considerable proportion of zinc (sometimes >1/3) to improve flow and give a fair golden colour. After casting, remove mould, cut off channels, and recover surplus metal for reuse. To estimate required metal, make and weigh a wax lump of the statue+channels, cast a metal lump of the same size, weigh both and compute metal-to-wax ratio to determine how much metal to melt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and placement rules for channels and vents in statue casting
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide both many small channels (cccc) on the wax statue entering larger channels (ddd) that meet at a single pouring hole, and include one or two vents to let out air (ff) and holes at the foot (gg) for wax drainage and later sealing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place great channels both upright and transverse so they meet at the top; ensure channels are sized and positioned for easy distribution of metal and for air escape to prevent voids. Expect more metal to be contained in channels than in the thin statue itself; plan economical channel geometry accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engineering responses and design principles for Papin's rarefaction water-raising engine
rubrics_metrics.description: Address objections regarding receptacle overfilling, the large quantity of air to rarefy, feasibility of raising water >32 feet, and pipe-filling issues: propose letting inferior receptacles overflow via crooked pipes with valve-controlled lower apertures; design wheel/pumps to rarefy the required air volumes by suitable rotational velocity; use as many pumps as receptacles for long distances; raise water stepwise between receptacles (~12 feet per stage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prevent overfilling, insert a crooked pipe in each receptacle reaching downwards with a valve to let out water when filled to a given height. For the large quantity of air, arrange the wheel with axis speed so air under ascending plugs is sufficiently rarefied (example computations yield air velocities and distances). For long lifts, many receptacles/pumps are required but metal costs remain low because external pressure does most work and heavy strength to resist internal pressure is not needed. It suffices that water moves into each next upper receptacle; the mechanism of getting it there (rarefaction or otherwise) is secondary so long as the pressure differences are adequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulates and method for modelling air resistance (Wallis' lemma)
rubrics_metrics.description: Postulate that, all else equal, the air's resistance to bodies is proportional to velocity (celerity). Represent impressed force as 1, resistance as r, effective force at first moment 1 - r; model successive equal time moments by multiplicative attenuation leading to a geometrical progression whose sum yields the net distance/effect compared to the no-resistance case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the geometric-progression formalism to compute the aggregate effect of continuous resistance (derive remaining fraction as 1/(m) etc.). Be aware of the caveat (noted in the text) that the first postulate is erroneous: atmospheric resistance is at least proportional to the square of the velocities in many regimes, and additional resistance from tenacity/viscosity and particle interactions must be considered; proper deduction or experiment is needed to discover the correct compound function of velocity.
